AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar

AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar

Nathaniel Cohen    Nicolas Dufour    Amélie Royer    Alasdair Newson    Patrick Pérez
Abstract

Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.720.7 fps for a 1616 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720720p video at 9.79.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher’s trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23×23\times faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720720p while running 17×17\times faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 3030K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.

1 Introduction

Recent speech-to-speech models [12, 41] are able to model full-duplex voice interaction in real-time, paving the way for voice assistants that hold natural and smooth conversations. However, these models only generate audio signal. In contrast, human spoken communication relies on visual cues and facial expressions, via an interplay of the audio and visual modalities. For instance, lip motion alters perceived phonemes [36], visual cues sharpen comprehension in noise [47], and an embodied talking face enhances the sense of social presence over voice alone [6]. To model such behaviors, audio-driven video generation models can synthesize talking-head videos from a reference image and an input speech audio, enabling applications such as virtual avatars, synthetic presenters, and non-player characters in games. All these applications, however, share a common constraint: the avatar must be generated on-the-fly, as the audio arrives, from a stream of audio of unbounded duration.

State-of-the-art talking-head models such as TalkVerse [52] and Wan-S2V [17] produce high-quality audio-driven videos but are ill-suited to the streaming setting. Because they rely on bidirectional attention, they must generate entire video chunks of several seconds at once, running dozens of denoising steps over the full chunk before producing any frame, which on a single GPU takes minutes per chunk. Recently, CausVid [59] and Self-Forcing [23] have explored distilling such bidirectional video diffusion teachers into few-step causal students that generate video chunk by chunk in an autoregressive manner. However, these methods target only the text-to-video and image-to-video settings. Extending this approach to the audio-driven setting, where the model must additionally track a dense time-aligned speech signal, has so far been demonstrated only on much larger models (14–18B parameters)  [24, 42, 33], which remain too large for real-time inference on a single GPU (only 2 fps). A second obstacle is the scarcity of suitable training data: existing public talking-head datasets such as Hallo3 [9] and CelebV [63] consist of clips too short to cover the chunk length of modern teachers like TalkVerse, ruling them out for distillation (see Section 3.6).

We introduce AURA, a family of causal few-step speech-to-video (S2V) models that generate streaming talking-head videos from live audio. In particular, AURA 1.3B runs in real time, generating 576576p video at 20.720.7 frames per second for a 1616 Hz playback rate on a single GPU, which makes it directly usable for the interactive applications above, such as a talking face for a voice assistant. AURA 5B targets higher resolution: it streams 720720p video at 9.79.7 fps, a 17×17\times speedup over its TalkVerse teacher. For training, we generate and release a new talking-head dataset comprising 3030K videos (38.738.7 hours) produced with TalkVerse, conditioned on reference images and text descriptions from the Hallo3 dataset [9] and synthetic speech audio. To train our model, we use a two-stage distillation pipeline, similar to CausVid: Stage 1 first trains the causal student to match the bidirectional TalkVerse teacher’s Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) trajectories in order to reduce the gap between the bidirectional teacher and the causal student architecture. Then, Stage 2 closes the few-step gap with Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) and backward simulation: by training the student on intermediate states from its own denoising rollouts, the Stage 2 loss reflects accumulating errors the student may actually produce at inference. To further improve efficiency, we train the model to support chunk-wise causal sliding window attention, allowing us to use a rolling KV cache with bounded memory at inference. We also use a single KV cache for all diffusion denoising timesteps, further reducing memory footprint.

With this approach, on standard talking-avatar benchmarks, AURA 5B matches or improves on its bidirectional teacher on visual quality (FVD [50] and JEDi [34] metrics) and audio-visual alignment, while running 17×17\times faster with only four denoising steps per chunk, and AURA 1.3B reaches a comparable quality at a lower resolution and in real time (23×23\times faster than its own teacher). Both models are faster than all baselines we compare against in the same single-GPU setting. Figure 1 shows an excerpt of qualitative samples generated by both models, as well as their speed–quality tradeoff against prior work.

In summary, we introduce AURA, which makes the following contributions:

  • •

    A two-stage distillation method (ODE-trajectory initialization followed by Distribution Matching Distillation with backward simulation) paired with a streaming inference scheme based on a rolling KV cache of past chunks, shared by both models;

  • •

    AURA 5B, a causal few-step S2V model that matches or improves on its bidirectional teacher on FVD and JEDi metrics, with a 17×17\times speedup. Our inference pipeline streams 720720p video at 9.79.7 fps on a single GPU, the highest throughput among audio-driven baselines we compare against;

  • •

    AURA 1.3B, a smaller model trained with the same pipeline, which streams 576576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.720.7 fps generated for a 1616 Hz playback rate), a 23×23\times speedup over its own bidirectional teacher;

  • •

    A public dataset of 3030K talking-head videos generated by TalkVerse from synthetic speech, released both as decoded videos and as the latent ODE trajectories of the teacher, to support future research on streaming S2V distillation, together with the weights of our 1.31.3B teacher and its own 3030K ODE trajectories;

  • •

    A live demo coupling AURA 1.3B with Unmute, a cascaded voice assistant built on Kyutai’s streaming speech-to-text and text-to-speech models [60] and a text LLM, in which users hold a natural spoken conversation with a synthetic avatar in real time on a single H100 GPU, available at kyutai.org/aura.

2 Related Work

Diffusion and Flow Matching.

Image Generative models have evolved through several paradigms: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [18, 25, 4] are efficient as they generate images in a single forward pass but suffer from known limitations around mode coverage and training stability. More recently, diffusion models [20, 45, 15, 44, 40, 26] and flow matching [30, 32] have become the dominant paradigm for image generation. Indeed, both frameworks are closely related and model data through an iterative multi-step refinement process, yielding stable training with high sample diversity but at the cost of slow sampling. Most modern large-scale video generators, including our teacher TalkVerse [52], are trained under the flow matching framework, and our work also builds on this formulation.

Video Diffusion Models.  Recent work has further scaled diffusion for video generation. Early efforts such as Imagen Video [21], Make-A-Video [43], Align Your Latents [3], and Stable Video Diffusion [2] extended image diffusion to short clips, typically by inflating 2D architectures with temporal layers. More recent open-source and industrial models, Sora [5], Movie Gen [38], Open-Sora [62], CogVideoX [56], HunyuanVideo [27], and Wan [51]— adopt diffusion transformer (DiT) architectures and operate in a compressed latent space, scaling to 720720p–10801080p resolutions and minute-long clips. These models are typically non-causal: they generate the entire video sequence jointly over 5050 or more denoising steps, and are thus not well adapted to the latency requirements of streaming applications. Current SotA talking-head models are based on such architectures. For instance, Hallo3 [9] adapts CogVideoX [56] for portrait animation with a DiT-adapted identity reference network, while closed-source systems such as OmniHuman [29] extend DiT-based audio-driven generation to full-body animation. In this work, we distill two such non-causal teachers built on Wan, TalkVerse [52] (from Wan2.2-5B) for AURA 5B and a 1.31.3B teacher that we train from Wan2.1-1.3B for AURA 1.3B, into causal, few-step streaming students.

Distillation of Diffusion Models.  The slow inference of diffusion models has motivated extensive work on distillation, training a faster few-step student to reproduce a slow teacher’s output distribution. One particularly successful line is Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [58], which trains a one-step student to minimize the reverse KL to the teacher via a learned critic; DMD2 [57] extends it to a few-step generator and introduces backward simulation, computing the loss on the student’s own rollouts rather than forward-diffused data. CausVid [59] applies DMD to distill a non-causal video teacher into a causal few-step student for streaming text-to-video. A challenge specific to causal video distillation is the train/test gap: the student is trained on teacher-provided past frames but must condition on its own previously generated frames at inference. Self-Forcing [23] and its variants [10, 64, 31, 54] address this temporal gap by rolling the student out autoregressively through a training-time KV cache with stop-gradient. We instead build on DMD2’s backward simulation [57], which exposes the student to its own denoising trajectory, and adapt it to streaming video (Sec. 3.4) so that the student also conditions on its own past generations, without maintaining a training-time cache.

Streaming Talking Heads.  A handful of recent works tackle audio-driven talking-head generation in a streaming and few-step setting. Talking Machines (Low and Wang, 2025) is, to our knowledge, the first to address this regime, distilling a 1818B model with DMD and sparse causal attention; weights are not released. Live Avatar (Huang et al., 2026b) distills the 1414B Wan-S2V model Gao et al. (2025) into a 1414B few-step student that runs at 1616 fps and 480480p on a 55-GPU setup. SoulX-FlashTalk (Shen et al., 2026) adopts a similar few-step distillation strategy from a 1414B teacher into a 1414B student and requires 44 GPUs to reach real-time throughput. In contrast, AURA streams on a single GPU: AURA 5B distills a 55B teacher into a same-size causal 44-step student that delivers 720720p video at 9.79.7 fps, and AURA 1.3B, trained with the same pipeline from our own 1.31.3B teacher, reaches real time at 576576p (20.720.7 fps for a 1616 Hz playback rate). Closest to our work is Avatar Forcing (Cui et al., 2026b) whose pre-print was concurrently published: It uses a similar DMD-based distillation process but requires a look-ahead window of future audio to generate each frame by design, leading to a small yet incompressible streaming delay.

3 Method

In this section, we present AURA, our two-stage pipeline that distills a non-causal audio-driven video diffusion teacher (TalkVerse) into a 44-step causal student. We first recall Distribution Matching Distillation (Sec. 3.1) and the TalkVerse teacher (Sec. 3.1) to introduce necessary notations and context. Section 3.2 then introduces the causal student and the per-chunk mixed-timestep design that enables a compact KV cache. Section 3.3 and Section  3.4 cover the two training stages, and Section 3.5 finally describes streaming inference.

3.1 Preliminaries

Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD).

DMD (Yin et al., 2024b) trains a few-step student generator GθG_{\theta} to match a multi-step teacher diffusion model at the distribution level, rather than along individual sampling trajectories. Concretely, DMD minimizes, in expectation over the diffusion timestep t∼𝒰⁡(0,1)t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1), the reverse KL divergence between the student distribution pgenp_{\text{gen}} and the data distribution pdatap_{\text{data}}, both diffused to noise level tt. We adopt t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] throughout this paper, with t=0t=0 corresponding to clean latents and t=1t=1 to pure noise. While the densities pgenp_{\text{gen}} and pdatap_{\text{data}} are intractable, the gradient of the KL with respect to θ\theta admits a closed-form expression as a difference of two score functions evaluated on student samples:

∇θℒDMD\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{DMD}} ≜𝔼t[∇θKL(pgen,t∥pdata,t)]\displaystyle\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[\nabla_{\theta}\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\text{gen},t}\,\|\,p_{\text{data},t}\bigr)\bigr]
≈−𝔼t∫(sdata(Ψ(Gθ(z),t),t)−sgen,η(Ψ(Gθ(z),t),t))d​Gθ​(z)d​θdz,\displaystyle\approx-\mathbb{E}_{t}\int\bigl(s_{\text{data}}(\Psi(G_{\theta}(z),t),t)-s_{\text{gen},\eta}(\Psi(G_{\theta}(z),t),t)\bigr)\frac{dG_{\theta}(z)}{d\theta}\,dz, (1)

where zz denotes the noise input to the student, Ψ⁡(⋅,t)\Psi(\cdot,t) is the forward diffusion operator that produces a sample at noise level tt, sdatas_{\text{data}} is the frozen teacher score, and sgen,ηs_{\text{gen},\eta} is an online score network (called critic in this paper) with parameters η\eta that estimates ∇log⁡pgen,t\nabla\log p_{\text{gen},t} on student samples. In practice, sgen,ηs_{\text{gen},\eta} is trained jointly with GθG_{\theta} via the standard denoising score-matching loss on student samples, and the two are updated in an alternating fashion.

Backward simulation.  Directly applying DMD to multi-step students yields a training-inference mismatch: at training time, the student is fed forward-diffused real samples xt=Ψ⁡(x0,t)x_{t}=\Psi(x_{0},t), whereas at inference time, intermediate inputs come from previous denoising steps of the student itself. To close this gap, DMD2 (Yin et al., 2024a) introduces backward simulation. At each training iteration, the student is unrolled for a few denoising steps to produce a synthetic intermediate sample x^t\hat{x}_{t}, which then replaces the forward-diffused real sample as input to the DMD objective. Because GθG_{\theta} is itself a few-step generator, this unrolling is cheap. The DMD gradient and the score-matching update for sgen,ηs_{\text{gen},\eta} are then computed at x^t\hat{x}_{t} rather than at Ψ⁡(x0,t)\Psi(x_{0},t), aligning the input distribution seen during training with the one produced at inference. DMD2 also adds a GAN loss on real data. We adopt backward simulation, together with the two time-scale update rule of DMD2, in the second stage of our pipeline (Sec. 3.4), but not the GAN loss: it requires real videos and makes training less stable. The DMD objective alone already brings our student close to its teacher (Sec. 4.3).

TalkVerse Architecture.  We use TalkVerse Wang et al. (2025) as our teacher model, a 55B-parameter audio-driven video diffusion model built on the Wan2.2-5B Wan et al. (2025) DiT backbone. Its video VAE uses compression factors (t,h,w)=(4,16,16)(t,h,w)=(4,16,16), enabling efficient 720720p generation. The model is conditioned on a reference identity image, a speech audio track encoded with Wav2Vec2 Baevski et al. (2020) and injected via cross-attention to temporally aligned visual tokens, and a text prompt encoded with T5-XXL Raffel et al. (2020). Long videos are generated with a sliding-window mechanism that conditions each window on a set of motion frames compressed by a FramePack module Zhang et al. (2026), and the reference image is assigned a positional offset placed ahead of the denoised window. Inference uses 5050 denoising steps with a flow-matching solver and classifier-free guidance. We provide a more detailed description in the supplementary material A.1. TalkVerse is directly the teacher of AURA 5B; for AURA 1.3B, we train a 1.31.3B teacher with the TalkVerse pipeline (Sec. 4.1 and supplementary material A.4).

3.2 AURA Architecture

To turn the 5050-step bidirectional teacher (TalkVerse) into a 44-step causal student, we introduce three architectural modifications: chunked causal sliding window attention, removal of motion frames, and per-chunk mixed timesteps. In combination, these changes also enable us to keep a compact rolling KV cache as illustrated in Figure 2b.

Chunked causal attention.  The student generates videos in chunks of nc=4n_{c}=4 latent frames (∼0.64\sim 0.64 s at the 2525 Hz native rate), whereas the teacher generates 3030 latent frames (∼5\sim 5 s) in a single pass. We enforce causality between chunks in the student: during training, a block-wise causal attention mask prevents frames in chunk CiC_{i} from attending to frames in chunks CjC_{j} for j>ij>i, while attention is bidirectional within a chunk (Figure 2a).

No motion frames.  TalkVerse normally conditions each generated video sequence on a window of past frames (motion frames) to maintain temporal coherence across windows. In our causal student, the KV cache already carries the past context required for coherence, thus we remove the motion frame mechanism entirely. This also saves us the cost of a few forward passes through the model required to process motion frames for every new chunk.

Per-chunk mixed timesteps: a compact KV cache.  At 720720p, the KV cache is already large at a single noise level due to the high spatial token count per frame. A naive implementation that would scale one (temporal) KV cache per diffusion step would increase the memory cost by the number of denoising steps per chunk. To avoid this, we train the model to handle sequences in which different chunks are at different noise levels: each chunk is assigned a single diffusion timestep tit_{i}, shared by all frames within the chunk (Figure 3, center). This per-chunk mixed timesteps scheme follows CausVid Yin et al. (2025), which adopts it without explicit motivation. We argue it is a key design choice to enable a compact streaming KV cache. At inference, the current chunk is fed at a high noise level tcurrt_{\mathrm{curr}} while previously generated chunks, cached in the KV cache, are at the lowest noise level reached during their own generation. The cache therefore stores keys and values at a single low noise level per past chunk, rather than at every diffusion step (Fig. 2(b)). In contrast, prior streaming audio-driven models that retain multiple noise levels in the cache pay a proportional memory cost Huang et al. (2026b).

3.3 Stage 1: ODE Teacher Forcing

As reported in CausVid Yin et al. (2025), directly applying DMD to a causal student starting from teacher weights is unstable as the student differs architecturally from the teacher. Therefore, we adapt their ODE-distillation initialization strategy to our setting. Stage 1 trains the causal student to follow the teacher ODE under the new architecture (Figure 3, top), bringing the student close enough to the teacher distribution so that Stage 2 can converge.

Training data.  We train Stage 1 on our synthetic dataset described in Section 3.6. Each video comes with latents stored at five timesteps along a 5050-step ODE trajectory from the teacher. At training time, the student is queried at the four timesteps {0.25,0.5,0.75,1}\{0.25,0.5,0.75,1\} and supervised to predict the clean latent at t=0t=0.

Training objective.  For each training video, we independently sample a noise level for each chunk uniformly at random from the four cached non-zero timesteps, following the per-chunk mixed timestep scheme of Section 3.2. This matches the heterogeneous-noise configurations the student encounters at inference, where the current chunk is noisy while past chunks (in the KV cache) are near-clean (at lowest noise level). The student processes the resulting sequence under the block-wise causal mask and predicts a velocity field vθ​(zt,t,c)v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c), where ztz_{t} denotes the noised latent at level tt (Section3.1) and cc denotes the text, audio and identity conditioning. From the predicted velocity we reconstruct the clean latent x^0\hat{x}_{0} and apply an MSE loss directly on x^0​(zt,t,c)\hat{x}_{0}(z_{t},t,c) rather than on the velocity. The Stage 1 loss reads:

ℒstage1=𝔼t,zt,c​[‖x^0​(zt,t,c)−x0‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\text{stage1}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,z_{t},c}\left[\big\|\hat{x}_{0}(z_{t},t,c)-x_{0}\big\|_{2}^{2}\right], (2)

where x0x_{0} is the clean latent produced by the teacher. The objective is to match the clean latents of the teacher, not the full flow trajectory: at inference, the 44-step student does not integrate the velocity field but alternates between x^0\hat{x}_{0} prediction and renoising (see A.2).

3.4 Stage 2: Backward Simulation DMD

Stage 1 yields a causal few-step student that closely follows teacher ODE trajectories, but its sample quality remains bounded by the compression from many-step to few-step inference. In Stage 2 we apply the DMD objective introduced in Section  3.1 (Equation (1)) to push the student output distribution toward the teacher distribution, with a sampling strategy adapted to our causal, chunked setting (Figure 3, bottom).

Models.  We maintain three networks: the frozen teacher fteacherf_{\text{teacher}}, the trainable student GθG_{\theta} (initialized from Stage 1), and a trainable critic fϕf_{\phi} that estimates ∇log⁡pgen,t\nabla\log p_{\text{gen},t}, playing the role of sgen,ηs_{\text{gen},\eta} in Equation (1). Following the two time-scale update rule of DMD2 (Yin et al., 2024a), the critic is initialized from the teacher and updated U=5U=5 times between each student update.

DMD objective.  Applying Equation (1) to our setup, the student gradient becomes

∇θℒDMD=𝔼t,x^0​[(fϕ​(x^t,t)−fteacher​(x^t,t))​∂x^0∂θ],x^0=Gθ​(z,c),\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{DMD}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,\hat{x}_{0}}\left[\big(f_{\phi}(\hat{x}_{t},t)-f_{\text{teacher}}(\hat{x}_{t},t)\big)\frac{\partial\hat{x}_{0}}{\partial\theta}\right],\quad\hat{x}_{0}=G_{\theta}(z,c), (3)

where zz is the noise input, cc denotes the conditioning (audio, prompt, and reference image), t∼𝒰⁡(0,1)t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) indexes the diffusion noise level, and x^t=Ψ⁡(x^0,t)\hat{x}_{t}=\Psi(\hat{x}_{0},t) is the forward-diffused student sample at level tt. The two terms inside the bracket correspond, respectively, to the estimated student score and the teacher score, and their difference approximates the gradient of the reverse KL divergence KL(pgen,t∥pdata,t)\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{gen},t}\,\|\,p_{\text{data},t}) (Section 3.1). The critic fϕf_{\phi} is trained jointly with GθG_{\theta} via the standard denoising score-matching loss on student samples.

Backward simulation.  A central question in few-step distillation is which samples x^0\hat{x}_{0} to use when computing the DMD gradient. We adopt the backward simulation strategy of DMD2 (Yin et al., 2024a) (Sec. 3.1) and apply it to our causal, chunked student. At each iteration, we proceed in three steps: (i) we run a full multi-step rollout of GθG_{\theta} without backpropagation to obtain the intermediate noisy states {x^tk}\{\hat{x}_{t_{k}}\} (tk∈{0.25,0.5,0.75,1}t_{k}\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75,1\}) along its own sampling trajectory; (ii) we re-feed these states through GθG_{\theta} with gradients enabled, using per-chunk mixed timesteps (Sec. 3.2) sampled uniformly across the trajectory; (iii) we evaluate the DMD gradient (Eq. 3) at the resulting x^0\hat{x}_{0} (Figure 3, bottom). The student is thus supervised at the intermediate states it encounters at inference, reducing the training–inference mismatch.

3.5 Inference: Causal Generation with rolling KV Cache

At inference, the student generates the video autoregressively, one chunk of 44 latent frames at a time, in 44 diffusion steps per chunk. Within each chunk, we adopt the predict-and-renoise scheme of DMD2 (Yin et al., 2024a) (see supplementary material A.2). To extend generation to longer sequences, we use a rolling KV cache with a first-chunk anchor that provides temporal context across chunks, and a RoPE Su et al. (2024) re-indexing scheme that bridges training and inference.

Rolling KV cache.  The sampling scheme of DMD2 describes the denoising of a single chunk. To generate longer videos, each new chunk must attend to previously generated chunks for temporal coherence. A naive KV cache that stores keys and values for all previously generated chunks would grow linearly with video length. We instead use a rolling cache of fixed size matching our sliding window attention training:

  1. 1.

    the first chunk is kept as a fixed anchor that subsequent chunks always attend to. This mirrors the attention sink mechanism used to stabilize streaming language models (Xiao et al., 2024) and also often adopted for streaming long-video generation (Liu et al., 2026);

  2. 2.

    the latest nn chunks (n=1n=1 in our setting), which provide the immediate temporal context for local motion continuity. We keep a single past chunk (n=1n=1): enlarging the window to n=2n=2 does not improve quality overall while increasing cache size and lowering throughput (supplementary material, Table 11).

All other chunks are evicted from the cache once they fall outside this window, which yields constant inference memory regardless of video duration. Moreover, thanks to the per-chunk mixed-timestep training described in Section 3.2, cached entries only need to store keys and values at the lowest noise level reached at the last denoising step of the chunk, rather than at every diffusion step. The same attention pattern is reproduced at training time by the block-causal mask (Figure 2(a)), in a single forward pass and without maintaining a KV cache.

RoPE indexing.  At inference, generated-frame positions grow without bound, while the reference frame is anchored at a fixed temporal RoPE position 1010 to 4040 latents ahead of the current generation front at training time (Section  3.1 and supplementary material A.1). To preserve this training-time configuration, we explore a scheme to re-index the reference every 3030 new generated latent frames, in the spirit of the re-indexed reference or sink frames of recent streaming avatar models Huang et al. (2026b); Li et al. (2026); Cui et al. (2026b), shifting it by +30+30 each time so that its offset relative to the generation front cycles between +40+40 and +10+10 (Figure  8 in supplementary material). This keeps the relative position of the reference within the regime the model was trained on, and avoids the position drift that would otherwise accumulate over long autoregressive rollouts. In practice, we find that this reindexing design helps stabilizing long generation for AURA 5B. For the smaller AURA 1.3B however, it is more beneficial to directly cap the RoPE positions of the generated frames to the range seen in training in our experiments, as Anchor Forcing Yang et al. (2026) and StreamAvatar Sun et al. (2026) do (supplementary material A.4).

3.6 Synthetic Talking-Head Dataset

We find that existing audio-driven video datasets are ill-suited to our training setup: the TalkVerse training set is released only as YouTube URLs and is difficult to obtain reliably, while the Hallo3 dataset Cui et al. (2025) contains clips too short to match our teacher’s single-chunk generation window of ∼5\sim 5 s. We instead build a synthetic dataset by running the TalkVerse teacher on conditioning inputs we control, and release it to support Stage 1 ODE teacher forcing (Section 3.3) and future work on audio-driven distillation.

Conditioning inputs.  We draw reference images and their associated text prompts from Hallo3 dataset (Cui et al., 2025), and pair each (image, prompt) to a synthetic speech track: We first obtain textual English audio transcripts of Youtube videos provided in the LiveCC dataset Chen et al. (2025). Then, we generate speech from a subset of these transcript using an off-the-shelf text-to-speech model Zeghidour et al. (2025). The resulting clips average 4.84.8 s, matching the teacher’s chunk size.

Video generation.  For each (image, prompt, audio) triplet, we run the TalkVerse teacher at 720720p and 2525 Hz with 5050 ODE steps and a guidance scale of 4.54.5. Reference image quality is heterogeneous across Hallo3, which also leads to diverse quality in the resulting video clips; No quality filtering is applied. For each generated video, we also store the teacher’s latent ODE trajectory at five timesteps: the initial noise (t=1t=1), three intermediate states (t∈{0.75,0.5,0.25}t\in\{0.75,0.5,0.25\}), and the final clean latent (t=0t=0). Latents follow the TalkVerse VAE compression (4×16×164{\times}16{\times}16 over time and space). We additionally store the decoded clean videos as MP4 files alongside the original audio tracks.

Release.  The final dataset totals 30,00030{,}000 clips (38.738.7 h of synthetic videos, compared to ∼70\sim 70 h for Hallo3 and CelebV). We release the audio tracks, decoded videos, and the five-timestep latent ODE trajectories to foster reproducibility and future work on talking heads generation. TalkVerse is only available at 55B parameters. Since its training code is open source, we reuse its training pipeline to train our own 1.31.3B bidirectional teacher on a smaller Wan2.1 backbone (Sec. 4.1), which serves as the teacher of AURA 1.3B. We also release its weights and the 3030K ODE trajectories it generated for Stage 1 of AURA 1.3B (Sec. A.4).

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Architecture and initialization.

We train two students with the same recipe, building on the open-source TalkVerse codebase for training and inference. AURA 5B is initialized from its teacher, TalkVerse Wang et al. (2025) (55B parameters, built on Wan2.2 55B). AURA 1.3B is initialized from a 1.31.3B bidirectional speech-to-video teacher that we train ourselves with the TalkVerse training pipeline, adapting Wan2.1 1.31.3B text-to-video Wan et al. (2025) to speech as TalkVerse does from Wan2.2 55B, with LoRA adapters on the backbone and audio cross-attention layers. This teacher differs from TalkVerse in two ways. It is trained on much less data: 3131 h of real Hallo3 video (2323K clips), whereas TalkVerse is trained for about one epoch on its 6.36.3K-hour dataset. Its audio features come from the Mimi speech codec Défossez et al. (2024) instead of Wav2Vec2: Mimi is a more recent codec with a causal, streaming encoder, and we keep its first, semantic level (Sec. A.4 of the supplementary material). Both students are trained with LoRA adapters Hu et al. (2022) of rank 128128 on the attention layers. We additionally unfreeze their timestep embedding and output head, since our models use the per-chunk mixed-timestep scheme of Section 3.2 rather than the single shared timestep of the teachers. Both generate video in chunks of nc=4n_{c}=4 latent frames with 44 diffusion denoising steps per chunk. They differ in output resolution and rate: AURA 5B generates 720720p video (1216×7681216\times 768 or 960×960960\times 960, depending on the aspect ratio of the reference) played back at 2525 Hz, the native output rate of TalkVerse, and AURA 1.3B generates 576576p video (768×512768\times 512 or 576×576576\times 576, likewise) played back at 1616 Hz, the native rate of Wan2.1; we use fps (frames per second) elsewhere to denote throughput. Unless stated otherwise, experiments use AURA 5B.

Two-stage LoRA training.  Each stage trains its own LoRA adapters. At the end of Stage 1 (ODE teacher forcing), its LoRA is merged into the base weights, and Stage 2 (DMD with backward simulation) trains a fresh LoRA of the same rank, avoiding stacked adapters. The Stage 2 critic is initialized from the teacher, and only its LoRA adapters are trained. Both models use batch size 256256 and 55 critic updates per student update. AURA 5B runs Stage 1 for 120120K steps at learning rate 1e-5 and Stage 2 for 55K steps at 3.5e-7, on 6464 H100 GPUs. AURA 1.3B runs Stage 1 for 4040K steps at 1e-5, on trajectories of its own teacher, and Stage 2 for 6.56.5K steps at 2e-7, on 3232 H100 GPUs. Other hyperparameters, including the 1.3B teacher’s, are in the supplementary material (Sec. A.3, A.4).

Baselines.  We compare AURA against four open-source audio-driven avatar generation models. TalkVerse Wang et al. (2025) , our teacher, serves as a high-quality reference for the distillation. Wan-S2V 14B Gao et al. (2025) and Hallo3 Cui et al. (2025) are two recent large-scale non-causal S2V model. Live Avatar Huang et al. (2026b) is a streaming few-step approach and the closest competitor to AURA in inference regime. For all baselines we use the authors’ released code and checkpoints, and run inference under each method’s recommended settings.

Benchmarks.  We evaluate on two test sets we generate. Hallo3 test consists of 100100 first frames and prompts randomly sampled from the Hallo3 test set Cui et al. (2025), each re-paired with a real English speech track from an internal dataset to assess speaker generalization; all clips are 1010 s. CelebV-HQ test consists of 150150 first frames from CelebV-HQ Zhu et al. (2022), each paired with 88–2020 s of TTS-synthesized speech (same pipeline as Sec. 3.6) and the generic prompt “a person is talking”; we synthesize rather than reuse audio because CelebV-HQ clips are too short (∼\sim55 s) to test longer sequences.

Metrics.  We evaluate along five axes. Visual quality: FID (Heusel et al., 2017), FVD (Unterthiner et al., 2019) on 1616-frame windows, computed at three temporal offsets, @00 (initialization), @101101 and @109109 (windows centered on and starting at a mid-video chunk boundary, capturing inter-chunk discontinuities), and JEDi (Luo et al., 2025), an MMD-based distance on V-JEPA features more reliable at our limited sample counts, at the same offsets. The main tables report the mean over the three offsets, and the per-offset values are in the supplementary material (Sec. A.5). (The 1616-frame windows span 11 s at 1616 Hz and 0.640.64 s at 2525 Hz, so FVD and JEDi are only approximately comparable across output rates.) Temporal consistency: the warping error (WE), the mean L1 residual after RAFT (Teed and Deng, 2020) optical-flow alignment of consecutive frames, capturing flicker and chunk-boundary artifacts. Audio–visual alignment: Sync-C and Sync-D (Chung and Zisserman, 2016) (SyncNet). Identity preservation: CSIM, the mean cosine similarity between ArcFace (Deng et al., 2022) embeddings of the reference and generated frames. Inference timing: on a single H100100 GPU, generating one clip from a fixed 1010 s English audio and a 960×960960\times 960 reference at each model’s native resolution and frame rate; we report throughput (fps) for the DiT and VAE decoder separately and the end-to-end Total (excluding loading and warm-up). Total is not a simple composition of the two: for Live Avatar, offloading the DiT or VAE between calls to fit in GPU memory adds overhead.

4.2 Main Results

Quality and identity.  In Table 1 and 2 we report our main quantitative comparison against all baselines, alongside model size, output resolution, and number of diffusion steps. Despite using only 44 denoising steps instead of 5050, AURA matches or improves on its TalkVerse teacher across most automatic metrics, and is comparable to the much larger Wan-S2V (1414B, multi-step) on FVD, JEDi, and audio–visual alignment. On identity preservation (CSIM), AURA outperforms all baselines on both test sets (0.790.79 for AURA 5B and 0.840.84 for AURA 1.3B on Hallo3 test, 0.720.72 and 0.770.77 on CelebV-HQ test), which we attribute to our RoPE indexing schemes (Sec. 3.5) and to keeping the initial generated chunks in the rolling cache, both of which limit identity drift over long generations.

Speed.  Both AURA models are faster than all baselines, including Live Avatar, which is also a few-step model. Throughputs are reported in raw frames per second. AURA 5B, TalkVerse and Hallo3 generate at 2525 Hz, Live Avatar, Wan-S2V and AURA 1.3B at 1616 Hz. Measured in generated seconds of video per second of compute, AURA’s lead over the latter two is larger still. AURA 5B runs the end-to-end pipeline at 9.79.7 fps on a single H100100, a ∼𝟏𝟕×\mathbf{\sim 17\times} speedup over its TalkVerse teacher (0.580.58 fps); its diffusion transformer and VAE decoder alone reach 19.719.7 and 22.722.7 fps (on the DiT, a ∼𝟑𝟎×\mathbf{\sim 30\times} speedup over the teacher’s 0.690.69 fps), and the end-to-end throughput is bounded by their sequential composition. AURA 1.3B runs at 20.720.7 fps end-to-end (28.828.8 fps for the DiT, 96.996.9 fps for the VAE decoder), faster than its 1616 Hz playback rate: it streams in real time on a single H100100, a ∼𝟐𝟑×\mathbf{\sim 23\times} speedup over its bidirectional teacher (0.900.90 fps, measured on a single 4.84.8 s window since this teacher generates fixed-length clips). These timings use the square reference of our protocol (576×576576\times 576 output); at 768×512768\times 512, AURA 1.3B runs at 17.317.3 fps end-to-end, still faster than real time. Figure 1 (right) summarizes the quality–speed trade-off: AURA matches the best baselines on quality while being one to two orders of magnitude faster. Figure 6 in the supplementary material adds complementary visualizations.

Long-form streaming stability.  A central claim of AURA is that its rolling KV cache sustains generation over an unbounded stream at constant memory. To measure how quality and identity evolve over time, we run both models (44 steps) on the 100100 Hallo3 test references driven by 6060 s of speech and compute metrics on consecutive 1010 s segments (Figure 7 and Table 10 in the supplementary material). For AURA 1.3B, FVD and lip-sync stay flat over the six segments (FVD 179179–186186, Sync-C 4.734.73–4.814.81, no segment significantly different from the first), and so does identity for most videos (median per-video CSIM change −0.02-0.02 over the minute; a few videos drift and pull the mean from 0.830.83 to 0.780.78). AURA 5B degrades slightly after the first segment (FVD from 182182 to 195195–206206, then stable) and its identity drifts slightly (CSIM from 0.760.76 to 0.690.69).

Perceptual quality.  Distribution-based metrics (FID, FVD, JEDi) capture global feature statistics but do not penalize certain local artifacts: Hallo3 obtains the best FID, FVD, and JEDi on both test sets, yet its generations exhibit exaggerated mouth motion and recurrent hand artifacts that these metrics fail to flag (qualitative analysis in Fig. 9, supplementary material). To assess perceived quality directly, we run an anonymous human evaluation on the Mabyduck platform. We collected 400400 pairwise comparisons from 2727 raters on the 100100 Hallo3 test clips, covering all pairs among AURA 5B, AURA 1.3B, Hallo3 and our TalkVerse teacher, along four axes: overall visual quality, lip-sync, reference fidelity, and naturalness. Results are aggregated into per-axis Bayesian Elo scores (Fig. 4). Both AURA models are preferred over Hallo3 on all four axes, confirming that Hallo3’s distribution-metric lead does not translate into perceived quality. Against the non-causal 5050-step teacher, AURA 5B ranks higher on reference fidelity, consistent with our CSIM results, and is on par on visual quality, lip-sync and naturalness, despite being causal and ∼17×\sim\!17\times faster. AURA 1.3B also ranks above TalkVerse on reference fidelity, but below AURA 5B and TalkVerse on visual quality, which reflects its lower resolution, as well as on lip-sync and naturalness.

4.3 Ablations

We ablate the main design choices of our method. Unless stated otherwise, all ablations use the 5B student trained on the full pipeline and are evaluated on the Hallo3 test set with the same 1010 s clips as the main results (Sec. 4.2); the 44-step default row of each ablation is the AURA 5B row of Tab. 1. We add two diagnostics, defined in Sec. A.9 of the supplementary material: Sharp., the variance of the Laplacian of the aligned face (frame-level sharpness proxies are dominated by background and noise), and Δ\DeltaCol., a within-clip colour drift: how much further the mean colour of the face moves away from that of the reference face (distance in CIELAB) between the first (0.50.5–2.52.5 s) and last (7.57.5–9.59.5 s) two seconds.

Number of diffusion steps.  Table 3 reports quality metrics when generating each chunk in {1,2,3,4}\{1,2,3,4\} diffusion steps. Visually, videos become blurrier as the number of steps decreases (Sec. 4.4), which distribution metrics barely capture: FVD and JEDi are best at 44 steps and degrade only slightly at 33 and 22 steps, FID is even marginally better at 33 and 22 steps, and all drop clearly at 11 step. Face sharpness makes the blur explicit: it decreases monotonically from 50.450.4 at 44 steps to 37.537.5, 36.536.5 and 27.027.0 at 33, 22 and 11 steps. Identity (CSIM) and lip-sync remain essentially stable down to 22 steps; the lower warping error with fewer steps reflects the same blur, which leaves fewer details to flag as inconsistent across frames, rather than a real improvement. We adopt 44 steps in all other experiments as the best trade-off between per-frame quality and inference speed.

Stage 1 only vs. Stage 1 + Stage 2.  Table 4 compares a student trained only with ODE teacher forcing (Stage 1) against the full two-stage pipeline (Stage 1 + Stage 2). Adding the DMD stage substantially improves all perceptual quality metrics (FID, FVD, JEDi) and identity preservation (CSIM), confirming that Stage 1 alone is insufficient to close the gap to the teacher in the few-step regime. Lip-sync metrics also improve. As in the previous ablation, the temporal consistency metric (Warp) reaches lower value with Stage 1 only, but this reflects the same metric artifact on blurrier outputs rather than a real improvement: face sharpness is almost three times lower with Stage 1 only (18.318.3 vs. 50.450.4).

KV cache refresh with an additional step.  We tested three variants where an additional diffusion step is added at inference to refresh the KV cache with a less noisy state for the next chunk. Stage 1 is fine-tuned to additionally handle a low timestep t=0t=0 in its ODE trajectories, and Stage 2 is retrained from scratch with this extra low timestep included in the backward simulation: t=0t=0 in 5-step (t=0t=0 refresh) and t=50t=50 in the two 5-step (t=50t=50) variants. At inference, this extra step updates the cache for the next chunk; its output is discarded in the first two variants and used as the final chunk prediction in the third. Table 5 reports the results. None of the variants consistently outperforms the simpler 44-step default: FID and lip-sync slightly improve in some variants, but FVD, JEDi, and identity preservation are degraded, markedly for the two t=50t{=}50 variants (FVD ≈210\approx 210 vs. 195.5195.5, CSIM 0.740.74 vs. 0.790.79). These two variants also drift within the clip: the colour distance between the face and the reference grows by 3.13.1 over 1010 s (Δ\DeltaCol.; 0.40.4 for the default), a perceptible shift, the face getting brighter over time. Given the added inference cost, we keep the 44-step default.

Rolling-window size.  Keeping two past chunks in the rolling cache instead of one (n=2n=2, Tab. 11 and Sec. A.10 in the supplementary material) slightly improves FVD (193.2193.2 vs. 195.5195.5) but degrades JEDi, identity and lip-sync, while increasing cache size and lowering throughput; we keep n=1n=1.

4.4 Qualitative Results

Figures 1 and 5 show representative AURA generations, from both models, on different test sequences spanning varied lighting conditions, head poses, and identities. The generated frames remain faithful to the reference identity throughout the sequence, and exhibit natural motion patterns – including spontaneous eye blinks, subtle head movements, and small facial expression variations – that go beyond strict lip motion.

Figure 10 in supplementary material compares AURA 5B to its TalkVerse teacher on the same input. Despite using only 44 denoising steps instead of 5050, AURA matches the teacher’s visual quality, and in some cases improves over it: in the example shown, the TalkVerse output produces a static gaze with no blinking over the full 1010 s clip, whereas AURA generates natural eye blinks and more varied global motion. Full videos for all sequences, including AURA 1.3B samples, are on the project page at https://kyutai.org/aura/.

5 Conclusions

We present AURA, a family of causal few-step speech-to-video models for streaming talking-head generation. Distilling a bidirectional teacher into a same-size 44-step causal student through a two-stage pipeline and a rolling KV cache, AURA 5B matches or improves on its TalkVerse teacher on FVD and JEDi at a 17×17\times speedup, delivering 720720p video at 9.79.7 fps on a single GPU. AURA 1.3B, distilled with the same pipeline from a 1.31.3B teacher, streams 576576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.720.7 fps for a 1616 Hz playback rate). We also release a 30,00030{,}000-clip synthetic dataset with teacher ODE trajectories, as well as our 1.31.3B teacher and its ODE trajectories, to support future work on audio-driven distillation.

Appendix A Supplementary Material

A.1 TalkVerse

We use TalkVerse Wang et al. (2025) as the teacher of AURA 5B, a 5B-parameter audio-driven video generation model built on the Wan2.2-5B Wan et al. (2025) Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbone, originally pretrained for text-and-image-to-video generation. TalkVerse extends the Wan-S2V Gao et al. (2025) design for speech-conditioned video synthesis to the Wan2.2 backbone, and trades the 14B-parameter scale of Wan-S2V for a smaller 5B model, trained on a high-resolution open-source dataset.

Latent space.  TalkVerse uses the Wan2.2 video VAE, which downsamples by (t,h,w)=(4,16,16)(t,h,w)=(4,16,16), a higher compression ratio than the (4,8,8)(4,8,8) commonly used in prior video diffusion models (e.g. Wan2.1). This yields a 4×4\times reduction in latent token count at the same resolution, enabling efficient high-resolution (720p) generation.

Conditioning.  The model is conditioned on three inputs: (i) a reference identity image, (ii) a speech audio track, and (iii) a text prompt describing the video content. Audio is encoded with Wav2Vec2 Baevski et al. (2020) and injected into a subset of DiT blocks via cross-attention from visual tokens to audio tokens, with each latent frame attending to a temporally aligned audio segment. The text prompt is encoded with T5-XXL Raffel et al. (2020) and injected through cross-attention. TalkVerse is trained on the large-scale TalkVerse-2.3M dataset of high-resolution audio-synchronized clips.

Long-video generation: temporal context.  To generate minute-long videos, TalkVerse uses a sliding-window mechanism: each window denoises a fixed number of frames conditioned on a window of preceding frames, referred to as motion frames. To keep the token budget tractable, the motion frames are compressed by a FramePack module Zhang et al. (2026) and assigned negative positional embeddings to mark them as past context.

Long-video generation: reference frame placement.  The reference identity image is assigned a positional embedding placed after the denoised video window, specifically position 4040 for a denoised window of 3030 latent frames. This forward offset makes the model “chase” the reference rather than copy it, which the authors report avoids copy-paste artifacts and looped body movements when the same reference is reused across sliding windows.

Training and inference.  TalkVerse is trained with LoRA on the DiT attention layers, while audio projection, audio cross-attention, and FramePack-related modules are fully fine-tuned. Inference uses 50 denoising steps with a flow-matching solver and classifier-free guidance.

A.2 Sampling scheme

Within each chunk, we adopt the predict-and-renoise scheme of DMD2 (Yin et al., 2024a). Standard flow matching integration zt−Δ​t=zt+vθ​(zt,t,c)⋅Δ​tz_{t-\Delta t}=z_{t}+v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c)\cdot\Delta t assumes that intermediate states lie on the learned ODE trajectory, an assumption that breaks down in the few-step regime, where each step spans a large interval of noise levels. Given a schedule of K=4K=4 denoising steps with timesteps 1=t0>t1>⋯>tK=01=t_{0}>t_{1}>\cdots>t_{K}=0, the chunk is initialized as zt0∼𝒩⁡(0,I)z_{t_{0}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), and each step kk proceeds in two parts. The student first predicts the velocity vθ​(ztk,tk,c)v_{\theta}(z_{t_{k}},t_{k},c) and reconstructs an estimate of the clean latent under the linear flow matching parameterization:

x^0(k)=ztk−tk⋅vθ​(ztk,tk,c).\hat{x}_{0}^{(k)}=z_{t_{k}}-t_{k}\cdot v_{\theta}(z_{t_{k}},t_{k},c). (4)

This estimate is then re-noised to the next noise level tk+1t_{k+1} with fresh Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I):

ztk+1=(1−tk+1)⋅x^0(k)+tk+1⋅ϵ.z_{t_{k+1}}=(1-t_{k+1})\cdot\hat{x}_{0}^{(k)}+t_{k+1}\cdot\epsilon. (5)

The final latent of the chunk is x^0=x^0(K−1)\hat{x}_{0}=\hat{x}_{0}^{(K-1)}, obtained at the last denoising step. The re-noising in Eq. 5 projects each intermediate estimate back onto the manifold of noisy latents the student was trained on, rather than following a straight-line integration of the velocity field. The same scheme is used during Stage 2 training to roll out the student without backpropagation and produce the noisy states {x^tk}\{\hat{x}_{t_{k}}\} used by backward simulation (Sec. 3.4), keeping training and inference aligned.

A.3 Training Details

We implement the chunk-wise causal attention mask (sliding window plus initial-chunk sink, Fig. 2) with FlexAttention Dong et al. (2024), which compiles custom attention-mask patterns efficiently. This is only required at training, where attention spans the full sequence; at inference the rolling KV cache reduces attention to the cached chunks, so no custom masking is needed. Full optimizer settings, LoRA configuration, and per-stage schedules of AURA 5B are reported in Table 6 (AURA 1.3B: Sec. A.4).

A.4 AURA 1.3B

AURA 1.3B follows the AURA 5B recipe (chunk-wise causal mask, mixed per-chunk timesteps, rolling KV cache, two-stage distillation) on a smaller backbone, with its own bidirectional teacher. Hyperparameters are listed in Tab. 7.

Backbone and audio features.  The backbone is Wan2.1 1.31.3B text-to-video Wan et al. (2025) with its 1616-channel VAE (4×8×84{\times}8{\times}8 compression). Videos are generated at 1616 Hz in one of two shapes, 768×512768{\times}512 or 576×576576{\times}576, chosen from the aspect ratio of the reference image; a training clip covers 2020 latent frames (7777 frames, 4.84.8 s). Speech is encoded with the Mimi codec Défossez et al. (2024), keeping only its first, semantic quantization level as a continuous 512512-dimensional latent. Audio enters through cross-attention layers initialized from the text cross-attention layers.

Teacher.  The bidirectional teacher is trained with flow matching on 23,14723{,}147 real Hallo3 Cui et al. (2025) clips, each truncated to its first 2020 latent frames (4.84.8 s, 3131 h in total; 500500 clips held out for validation, none of the Hallo3 test clips), each with its own speech track, using LoRA adapters on the backbone and full-rank audio cross-attention. The loss is a flow-matching MSE weighted by face and body masks, and the audio, image and text conditions are each dropped with probability 0.10.1 for classifier-free guidance. We use the checkpoint at 6060K steps. Unlike TalkVerse, the teacher has no motion frames (no FramePack module): it is only used for distillation, which requires single 2020-latent windows, so it never has to extend a video beyond one window.

Stage 1 data.  Since the teacher is trained on real Hallo3 videos, we build its ODE trajectories on 3030K Hallo3 conditions (first frame, the clip’s own speech, and its caption, or the generic prompt “a person is talking” for 61%61\% of them), disjoint from Hallo3 test, with 5050 ODE steps and a guidance scale of 4.54.5.

Stage 1 and Stage 2.  Stage 1 regresses the teacher trajectories as for AURA 5B, with the clean timestep t=0t=0 included among the per-chunk timesteps, and LoRA adapters on the attention layers and on the audio layers. Stage 2 uses DMD with backward simulation on 9292K conditions (Hallo3 first frames and prompts paired with synthetic speech from the pipeline of Sec. 3.6, disjoint from Hallo3 test); the student audio adapters are frozen, and the generator is read from an exponential moving average of its weights (decay 0.990.99). We keep the EMA checkpoint at 6,5006{,}500 optimizer steps. At inference, AURA 1.3B uses the 44-step schedule of AURA 5B and re-indexes the RoPE positions of the generated frames so that they never exceed the range seen during training.

A.9 Diagnostic metrics for the ablations

The ablations (Sec. 4.3) use two diagnostics in addition to the metrics of Sec. 4.1, computed on the 100100 Hallo3 test clips (1010 s) and averaged over videos.

Face sharpness (Sharp.)  Variance of the 3×33{\times}3 Laplacian, a standard focus measure Pech-Pacheco et al. (2000), on the grey-level inner face (brows to chin, cheek to cheek). At 55 frames per second, the largest face (RetinaFace Deng et al. (2020), ResNet-50) is aligned on the ArcFace Deng et al. (2022) template at 256×256256{\times}256, so that its size does not depend on the output resolution; frames without a face are skipped. Higher is sharper. We do not use the whole frame: frame-level proxies (variance of the Laplacian, high-frequency FFT energy) are dominated by background texture and noise, and rank the 11-step and Stage-1-only models as the sharpest.

Colour drift (Δ\DeltaCol.)  How much further the face colour moves away from the reference over a clip. At 55 frames per second, we compute Δ​E\Delta E, the CIELAB distance between the mean colour of the inner face (detected and aligned as above, at 112×112112{\times}112) and that of the reference face. Δ\DeltaCol. is the mean Δ​E\Delta E over the last two seconds (7.57.5–9.59.5 s) minus the mean over the first two (0.50.5–2.52.5 s); lower is better. This follows the start-versus-end drift measure of FramePack Zhang et al. (2026) and Rolling Forcing Liu et al. (2026), restricted to the face and taken against the reference, hence signed. For scale, a Δ​E\Delta E of about 2.32.3 is commonly taken as a just-noticeable difference Mahy et al. (1994): the default model stays at Δ​E≈2\Delta E\approx 2 from the reference (Δ\DeltaCol. 0.40.4), whereas the t=50t{=}50 refresh variants drift by 3.13.1, to 5.75.7–5.85.8.

A.10 Rolling cache window size

We ablate the number of past chunks nn retained in the rolling KV cache (Sec. 3.5). Our default keeps a single past chunk (n=1n=1) alongside the first-chunk anchor; here we compare it against a larger window that also retains the second-to-last chunk (n=2n=2). The n=2n=2 variant is a dedicated 44-step student, whose Stage 2 is trained with the n=2n=2 attention mask; both are evaluated on Hallo3 test (1010 s clips). As reported in Table 11, enlarging the window to n=2n=2 slightly improves FVD (193.2193.2 vs. 195.5195.5) at an equal FID, but degrades JEDi, identity, lip-sync and warping error, while increasing cache size and lowering throughput. This supports our minimal single-chunk cache as the best quality–efficiency trade-off.
